title: The Lost Spring of Kettlebrook
markdown:
The sun burst over Kettlebrook, but the colours were not as bright. Worried whispers buzzed louder than bees. The stream — lifeblood of Kettlebrook and neighbour Sprout Hollow — was a sad muddy trickle. The world held its breath. Villages that had been as friendly as sunshine now glared across cracked dusty ground, voices sharp as dried reeds.

Lina Flickerwick was barely sixteen. Her eyes missed nothing. A knot in her stomach. Fingers itched for quills, for ink on parchment. Pretty maps would not bring water. Today she would chart a different path.

She exploded from her cottage. Crisp air slapped rosy cheeks, carrying baking bread from Mrs. Higgins's down the lane. Mission: the dusty cobwebbed den of Peregrine Blackwood. Captain Blackwood, they used to call him; the title had gathered dust. Whispers clung like burrs — botched expedition, lost patrol, a captain who'd lost his way. Lived like a grumpy badger. Perfect. Who she needed.

Determined kick. Creaky door. "Captain Blackwood! We need you!"

He was polishing a battered brass compass with almost violent intensity. Squinted with his one good eye; the other hid behind a faded somewhat comical patch. "Need me for what, kid? To tell you the sky's still blue, or the dirt's still brown and dusty?"

"The water!" She vibrated. "It's almost gone. They're talking of fighting. But I remember my grandfather's secret maps. A lost border path through the Whispering Orchard. A spring that never runs dry."

He scoffed; dust puffed from his scraggly beard. "The Whispering Orchard? Forbidden, Flickerwick. Prickly perils and grumpy grubs. Nobody's found that path in fifty years."

"But what if it is there? I need your eyes, Captain. A scout's eyes. Someone who knows how to truly look." She thrust an old parchment, edges softened with time.

His gaze flickered from map to her face. A tiny spark — curiosity? — in the single eye. "Prickly perils, you say?" A dry rusty chuckle that had not been heard in ages. "Alright, kid. You've got grit. Don't expect a grand adventure. Just a quick poke around a very prickly patch."

Therefore they went.

The Whispering Orchard was a wild tangled chaos. Ancient trees twisted like bony gnarled fingers. Their apples looked more like knobbly pebbles than anything edible. Big buzzing insects, fat as a thumb, flitted past, sweet cloying scent. Lina's heart hammered a frantic drumbeat. Tangled branches seemed to reach. Was this too much, too dangerous? She kept her focus glued to the map and the faint almost invisible marks Peregrine pointed out: tiny nicks carved into bark, small stones placed just so, the grammar of people who had needed to come home in the dark.

"See that?" he whispered, tapping a particularly twisted knobbly trunk. "Scout's mark. Older than your grandma's best hat. They used to mark the border, you know."

They pushed deeper, ducking under low-hanging branches that snagged clothes, boots crunching fallen leaves. Suddenly a rustle, loud and distinct, in the dense undergrowth. Two bulbous shiny eyes popped from behind thorny bushes. A Grumblebug. Lina knew the stories: fuzzy, incredibly grumpy, surprisingly sticky almost-invisible webs.

"Quick!" Peregrine hissed, grabbing her arm with surprising strength. "Don't make a sound." They froze, barely daring to breathe, chests tight. The Grumblebug shuffled past, long twitching antennae probing the air. Lina's breath hitched. A thread of web gleamed, then didn't. They waited until the undergrowth went still.

They pressed on, following increasingly faint markings, hopes dwindling with every vine and thorn. "Maybe your grandfather was just dreaming up stories," Peregrine muttered, frustration in the gruff.

But Lina remembered a different detail: a tiny cluster of dots that looked exactly like a spilled ink pot. "Wait! The spilled ink!" Sudden excitement, pointing. "It's not stars. It's a grouping of rocks!" She scrambled toward moss-covered boulders, boots slipping on damp earth. Behind them, hidden by a thick curtain of ivy, a narrow dark opening.

"The path!" His gruffness vanished. He pulled the ivy. A clear path into darker woods. Ahead, a soft sweet gurgle. Running water.

They burst into a sun-dappled clearing. A crystal spring bubbled, sparkling like a million tiny diamonds. "The Lost Spring," Lina whispered.

They raced back, spring water sloshing in Peregrine's canteen. Villagers already at the dry bed, angry words like sparks. A burly Sprout Hollow man picked up a hefty rock.

"Stop!" Lina's voice cut the din. She held up the canteen. "The lost border path is real. The spring is the source. There's enough for everyone."

Amazement. Peregrine, tall beside her, one eye gleaming: "The path is clear. The spring is yours, and ours. Enough for everyone. Always."

A cheer. Anger dissolving like mist. Hands shaking. Lina watched, a warm bubbling in her chest. She had charted a path not only on paper. Peregrine clapped her shoulder. "Well done, Flickerwick. Spirit of a true explorer."

She grinned. She did not declare the day AMAZING. She folded the map, ink-pot rocks and all, and thought of the next line she might draw, once the stream had remembered how to be a stream.
